title: Mentoring and Growing Other Architects
objectives: Develop the skills to mentor and grow the next generation of architects
Use the DDaT Capability Framework to structure development conversations
Create opportunities for less experienced architects to grow through stretch assignments
Build architecture communities of practice that foster collective learning
Transition from doing architecture to enabling others to do it well
whyThisMatters:
At senior levels in the DDaT Capability Framework, the expectation shifts from doing the work yourself to enabling others to do it. A Principal or Lead Solution Architect is measured not just by the quality of their own architecture decisions but by the quality of decisions made by the architects they influence, mentor, and develop.

Government has a persistent shortage of experienced architects. The DDaT capability framework defines the skills needed, but progression from associate to senior levels requires guided experience — learning from someone who has made the mistakes before and can help you make different ones. Without deliberate mentoring, architects learn slowly through trial and error, repeating avoidable failures.

The cross-government architecture community depends on people at senior levels investing time in those coming up behind them. Communities of practice, architecture guilds, peer learning groups, and one-to-one mentoring all require senior architects to share knowledge, provide feedback, and create safe spaces for less experienced colleagues to develop. This is not optional for senior architects — it is a core part of the role.

content.heading: The Senior Architect's Responsibility to Grow Others
content.body:
The DDaT Capability Framework makes this explicit. At senior and lead levels, architects are expected to mentor others, set standards, and develop the capability of their community. This is not something you do in your spare time — it is a core deliverable alongside your architecture work.

The transition from 'doing architect' to 'enabling architect' is uncomfortable for many. You became a senior architect because you are excellent at architecture. Now you are asked to spend significant time helping others become excellent — which means you are doing less architecture yourself. This feels like a loss of identity and impact. It is not. A senior architect who personally makes 10 excellent decisions per month has less organisational impact than one who helps 5 other architects each make 10 excellent decisions per month.

Your responsibility covers several dimensions:

Individual development: working one-to-one with less experienced architects to develop their skills, confidence, and judgement. This includes formal mentoring relationships, informal coaching during live work, and feedback on their architecture outputs.

Team capability: ensuring your architecture team collectively has the skills, knowledge, and practices to deliver high-quality work. This includes running design crits, establishing standards, sharing knowledge, and creating a culture where people learn from each other.

Community contribution: investing in the wider architecture community beyond your immediate team. This includes contributing to cross-government communities of practice, speaking at events, writing blog posts, and participating in peer review for other departments.

Succession: ensuring that your organisation's architecture capability does not depend solely on you. If you were hit by the proverbial bus, could the team continue? If the answer is no, developing others is urgent.

content.heading: Mentoring vs Coaching vs Teaching
content.body:
These three modes of developing others are different and suited to different situations. Effective senior architects use all three.

Mentoring is a longer-term relationship focused on career development and professional growth. A mentor shares their experience, helps the mentee navigate organisational challenges, provides perspective on career decisions, and acts as a sounding board for difficult situations. Mentoring is non-directive — you do not tell the mentee what to do; you help them think through their options and develop their own judgement.

Coaching is focused on specific skills or challenges. A coach helps someone improve their performance in a defined area — writing better ADRs, presenting more effectively to boards, improving their stakeholder management. Coaching is more directive than mentoring — you observe, provide specific feedback, and suggest techniques. Coaching relationships may be short-term (focused on a specific challenge) or ongoing (continued skill development).

Teaching is direct knowledge transfer. When someone needs to learn a specific technique, framework, or approach, you teach it — explaining the concept, demonstrating it, and providing guided practice. Teaching is appropriate for: government-specific knowledge (how spend controls work, how service assessments are structured), technical skills (architecture modelling techniques, security analysis methods), and domain knowledge (how a particular department's technology landscape works).

The most common mistake senior architects make is defaulting to teaching when they should be coaching or mentoring. When a less experienced architect brings you a problem, the temptation is to solve it for them (teaching). But if you always solve their problems, they never develop the judgement to solve their own. Better: ask questions that help them find the solution ('What options have you considered? What are the trade-offs? What would happen if...?'). This builds their decision-making capability, not just their knowledge of the specific answer.

content.heading: Using the DDaT Framework for Development Conversations
content.body:
The Government Digital and Data Profession Capability Framework provides a structured basis for development conversations with architects at all levels. It defines the skills expected at each level and the differences between levels — making it clear what someone needs to develop to progress.

For solution architects, the framework defines key skill areas including: availability and capacity management, development process optimisation, information security, making and guiding decisions, ownership and initiative, strategic thinking, technical understanding, and turning business problems into technical design. Each skill is defined at four proficiency levels: awareness, working, practitioner, and expert.

Using the framework in development conversations:

Start with self-assessment. Ask the architect to rate themselves against the framework for their current level. Where do they feel confident? Where do they feel they have gaps? Self-assessment reveals self-awareness — the most coachable people are those who accurately identify their own development needs.

Compare with observation. Your assessment of their strengths and gaps may differ from their self-assessment. Share your observations with specific examples. 'I notice you are strong at technical understanding but less confident presenting to non-technical boards — your recent presentation to the programme board used too much technical language and the board struggled to make a decision. Let us work on translating architecture into business language.'

Identify development actions. For each gap, discuss how to address it. Options include: stretch assignments (giving them work that requires the skill they are developing), shadowing (observing you or another senior architect in situations where the skill is needed), formal training (courses or workshops), peer learning (pairing with someone who is strong in that area), and reading/research (specific books, blogs, or government guidance).

Review regularly. Development is not a one-off conversation. Meet monthly or quarterly to review progress, celebrate growth, identify new challenges, and adjust the development plan. The architecture profession is continuously evolving — development needs change as the person grows and as government technology changes.

content.heading: Creating Stretch Opportunities
content.body:
People develop fastest when they are stretched slightly beyond their current capability — challenged enough to learn, but supported enough not to fail dangerously. Creating these opportunities deliberately is a key skill for senior architects.

Architecture review participation: invite less experienced architects to observe and then participate in architecture reviews. Start them as observers, then give them a section to lead (reviewing the security model, for example), then progress to leading a full review with your support.

ADR authorship: assign less experienced architects responsibility for writing ADRs for decisions within their service. Review and provide feedback. Progress from simple technology selection ADRs to more complex strategic decisions as confidence grows.

Presentation to boards: give less experienced architects opportunities to present architecture to non-technical audiences — first at low-stakes internal meetings, then at design authorities, then at programme boards. Coach them on preparation and provide feedback afterwards.

Cross-team architecture work: assignments that require working across multiple teams develop stakeholder management and communication skills that single-team work does not. Ask a developing architect to lead the integration architecture for a cross-team initiative.

Service assessment preparation: involve developing architects in preparing for GDS service assessments. This requires synthesising the full architecture story, anticipating assessor questions, and presenting under pressure. It is excellent development for articulating architecture reasoning.

Deputising for you: when you are unavailable (leave, other commitments), have a developing architect deputise for your governance role. Agree boundaries in advance (what they can decide alone, what they should defer until your return) and debrief when you return.

The key principle: stretch with support. Do not throw someone into a situation they are not ready for and hope they swim. Brief them beforehand (here is what to expect, here are common pitfalls), be available for questions during the work, and debrief afterwards (what went well, what was difficult, what would you do differently).

content.heading: Building Communities of Practice
content.body:
Individual mentoring develops individual architects. Communities of practice develop the collective capability of the architecture profession within and across organisations.

A community of practice is a group of people who share a profession or interest and learn from each other through regular interaction. The cross-government technical architecture community is an example — architects from across government connecting through Slack, regular meetups (architecture lunches and drinks), conferences (such as the 2025 Cross Government Software Engineering Conference), and blogs.

Within your department, an architecture community of practice might include:

Regular design crits: weekly or fortnightly sessions where architects present work-in-progress for peer feedback. Low-stakes, collaborative, focused on collective improvement rather than governance approval.

Knowledge sharing sessions: monthly presentations where someone shares something they have learned — a new pattern, a technology evaluation, a lessons-learned from an incident, or an explanation of a government framework that others may not understand.

Pair architecting: pairing a senior and developing architect on a piece of work — not just shadowing, but genuinely working together with shared responsibility. The senior architect coaches in real-time while the developing architect does the work.

Retrospectives on architecture decisions: quarterly review of ADRs from the past period, discussing which decisions were validated by outcomes and which turned out differently than expected. This normalises learning from experience — including learning from mistakes.

Book clubs or reading groups: reading and discussing architecture-relevant material together. Government-specific publications (NAO reports, CDDO guidance, GDS blog posts) are excellent material because they directly apply to the team's work.

For the community to thrive, it needs: protected time (people must be allowed to attend without guilt), senior support (leadership must visibly value participation), facilitation (someone must organise logistics, set agendas, and create psychological safety), and visible outcomes (the community must produce something — better architecture, shared patterns, documentation — that demonstrates its value).

content.heading: Giving Feedback That Develops
content.body:
Feedback is the mechanism through which mentoring and coaching create growth. Poor feedback either fails to develop (too vague, too infrequent, too positive) or actively harms confidence (too harsh, too personal, poorly timed).

Good development feedback is specific. Not 'your architecture documentation needs improvement' but 'your ADR for the database selection presented the options well but did not capture the consequences — readers cannot see what trade-offs you accepted. Add a consequences section that describes what becomes easier, what becomes harder, and what risks you have accepted.'

Good feedback is timely. Feedback given months after the event has little impact — the context has faded and the learning opportunity has passed. Provide feedback within days of the observed behaviour, while both you and the person remember the detail.

Good feedback balances reinforcement and challenge. People need to know what they do well (reinforcement) as much as what they need to improve (challenge). A pattern that works: 'Your presentation to the board was well-structured and clearly explained the options. The area to develop is handling pushback — when the finance director challenged your cost estimate, you became defensive rather than exploring their concern. Next time, try acknowledging their point first and then explaining your reasoning.'

Good feedback is about behaviour, not personality. 'Your presentation was unclear' is about behaviour — it can be changed. 'You are a poor communicator' is about personality — it feels like a judgement. Focus on observable actions and their impact.

Good feedback includes a forward path. Do not just identify the problem — suggest what to do differently. 'The security section of your architecture document was too brief. For the next document, try using the NCSC's Secure by Design principles as a structure — address each principle and explain how your architecture meets or mitigates it.'

Create regular feedback rhythms. Do not wait for formal review meetings. Build feedback into your regular interactions: brief comments after governance meetings, quick notes on reviewed documents, five-minute coaching conversations after presentations. Normalise feedback so that receiving it is not a special (anxiety-inducing) event.

workedExample.title: Developing a Mid-Level Architect to Senior Level
workedExample.context: A mid-level Solution Architect (HEO equivalent in DDaT) has been in the role for 3 years and wants to progress to senior level. They are technically strong — they design good solutions and write excellent ADRs. However, they struggle with stakeholder management (they default to technical language with non-technical audiences), they avoid conflict (they agree with pushback from delivery teams rather than defending their architecture position), and they have not led any cross-cutting architecture work. Their line manager has asked you, as the Lead Architect, to support their development.
workedExample.approach:
The Lead Architect designs a 6-month development plan using the DDaT framework as the structure.

Month 1-2 — Stakeholder Communication:
The developing architect shadows the Lead at two programme board presentations, noting how technical concepts are translated into business language. They then prepare and deliver a short architecture update to their own programme board, with the Lead providing coaching on preparation and feedback after delivery. The Lead shares a simple technique: for every technical concept, ask 'so what does this mean for users/cost/risk?' and lead with that answer.

Month 3-4 — Constructive Challenge:
The Lead assigns the developing architect to lead a design authority review of another team's architecture. This requires them to provide challenge — asking difficult questions and pushing back on weak reasoning. The Lead attends as an observer (not participant) and provides feedback afterwards. Key coaching: 'challenge is not conflict. Asking why is not attacking. Your questions today were good but too tentative — the team did not feel challenged and may not address the weaknesses you identified.'

Month 5-6 — Cross-Cutting Work:
The developing architect is given a cross-team initiative: defining the integration standards for three services that need to exchange data. This requires: getting agreement from three teams who have different preferences, presenting the standards proposal to the design authority, and handling disagreement when teams push back. The Lead provides background support (checking in weekly) but does not intervene unless requested.

Throughout — Regular One-to-Ones:
Fortnightly 30-minute sessions where the developing architect reflects on recent experiences, asks questions, and receives feedback. These sessions use the DDaT framework to track progress against specific skills: communication (improving), decision-making under uncertainty (emerging), and strategic thinking (to be developed in the next phase).
workedExample.outcome: After 6 months, the developing architect successfully presents to the programme board without coaching support, leads two design authority reviews with clear and constructive challenge, and delivers agreed integration standards for the cross-team initiative. They apply for a senior architect role in a different programme and are successful. In their new role, they cite the stretch assignments and coaching feedback as the most valuable development they received.
workedExample.lessonsLearned: The most impactful intervention was not teaching a technique but creating situations where the developing architect had to exercise skills they were uncomfortable with. The shadowing provided a model. The stretch assignments provided practice. The feedback provided course correction. The combination — model, practice, feedback — is more effective than any one approach alone. The Lead Architect invested approximately 4 hours per month in this development — a modest investment that produced a senior architect who would otherwise have taken years longer to develop.

civilServiceScenario.title: The Architecture Team With No Pipeline
civilServiceScenario.background: You are appointed as Lead Architect for a department with 4 solution architects — all at mid-level. The previous Lead left 8 months ago and was not replaced. In the interim, the team has continued doing project-level architecture but has lost: governance (no design authority meetings in 6 months), standards (each architect uses different patterns and documentation styles), community (no shared practices or learning), and strategic direction (no architecture roadmap or technology strategy). The CTO has asked you to rebuild the architecture practice while also delivering your own architecture work on a critical programme.
civilServiceScenario.challenge: You must rebuild team capability and practices while maintaining delivery. You cannot pause project work to focus on team development. You have no additional budget for training or external support. The four architects are competent at project-level work but have not had development focus or community for 8 months.
constraints: You are responsible for both delivery (a critical programme) and team development
Four mid-level architects with no recent development investment
No design authority or governance has operated for 8 months
Each architect works on a separate programme with different stakeholders
No budget for external training or coaching
The CTO expects visible improvement in architecture practice within 3 months
There is no succession — if you leave, the same problem recurs
The architecture team is physically distributed across 3 office locations
Some architects have developed informal practices that may conflict with what you establish
civilServiceScenario.yourRole: You are the newly appointed Lead Architect responsible for rebuilding the architecture practice.
civilServiceScenario.discussion:
This scenario tests the balance between delivery and development. You cannot stop delivering to build the practice, but you cannot ignore the practice because it will deteriorate further. The approach needs to be integrated — building practice through delivery rather than as a separate activity.

Practical starting points: reestablish a fortnightly design authority (even if attendance is initially just you and whoever is available), introduce a shared ADR template and repository (consistency through tooling), start fortnightly architecture community sessions (design crits, knowledge sharing, rotating facilitation), and establish monthly one-to-ones with each architect (development focus using DDaT framework).

Critically, you need to develop succession quickly — at least one of the four architects needs to be developing toward senior level so that the practice does not collapse again when you eventually move on. Identify the most promising candidate and begin the stretch assignment approach immediately.

practiceArtefact.description: Create a 6-month development plan for a mid-level Solution Architect who wants to progress to senior level. They are technically strong but need development in three areas: presenting to non-technical audiences, leading cross-team initiatives, and making architecture decisions under uncertainty. Use the DDaT Capability Framework as the structure.
practiceArtefact.guidance: For each development area, specify: the current state (what they can do now), the target state (what senior level looks like per the framework), specific development actions (shadowing, stretch assignments, coaching, training), success criteria (how you will know they have developed), and timeline. Include both formal and informal development activities.
practiceArtefact.modelAnswer:
**Architect Development Plan: [Name]**

Current Level: Mid-Level Solution Architect (SEO equivalent)
Target Level: Senior Solution Architect (G7 equivalent)
Timeline: 6 months | Reviewer: Lead Architect | Review Frequency: Monthly

**Development Area 1: Communication with Non-Technical Audiences**

DDaT Skill: Architecture Communication
Current State: Can explain architecture decisions clearly to technical colleagues. Struggles to translate for programme boards and senior leaders — defaults to technical language, loses audience engagement.
Target State (Senior): Can articulate architecture in terms of cost, risk, time, and value. Can present options and recommendations to investment committees and senior leaders. Adjusts communication style to audience.

Actions:
- Month 1: Shadow Lead Architect at 2 programme board presentations, noting communication techniques
- Month 2: Prepare and deliver a 5-minute architecture update at own programme board (Lead coaches on preparation, attends as observer)
- Month 3: Present an options paper to design authority in business language (not technical language)
- Month 4-6: Independently present architecture to programme boards without coaching
- Ongoing: After each presentation, debrief with Lead — what worked, what to change

Success Criteria: By month 6, consistently presents to non-technical audiences without defaulting to jargon. Board members can paraphrase the key message back.

**Development Area 2: Leading Cross-Team Initiatives**

DDaT Skill: Ownership and Initiative / Strategic Thinking
Current State: Works effectively within a single programme team. Has not led work that requires alignment across multiple teams with different priorities.
Target State (Senior): Can lead cross-cutting architecture work, negotiate between teams, and reach agreement on shared standards or patterns.

Actions:
- Month 2: Assign leadership of a cross-team integration standards piece (3 teams, low-stakes)
- Month 3-4: Coach through the stakeholder negotiation process as needed (available for questions, not solving problems directly)
- Month 5: Assign a more complex cross-team initiative with genuine disagreement to navigate
- Ongoing: Monthly reflection on what worked and what was difficult in cross-team leadership

Success Criteria: By month 6, has successfully delivered an agreed cross-team standard and can describe their approach to gaining alignment.

**Development Area 3: Decision-Making Under Uncertainty**

DDaT Skill: Making and Guiding Decisions
Current State: Makes good decisions when information is complete. Becomes stuck or defers when information is incomplete or ambiguous — waits for certainty rather than making progress with available information.
Target State (Senior): Comfortable making decisions with incomplete information. Distinguishes between decisions that need more data and decisions that need commitment. Uses techniques like time-boxing, reversibility assessment, and assumption documentation.

Actions:
- Month 1: Teach the concept of 'last responsible moment' and reversibility assessment
- Month 2-3: Assign a design decision with deliberate ambiguity — specify that a decision must be made within one week regardless of remaining uncertainty
- Month 4: Review the outcome — was the decision good enough? What would more information have changed?
- Month 5-6: Independently identifies decisions in their own work that need commitment rather than more analysis
- Ongoing: In one-to-ones, explicitly discuss decisions they are stuck on and explore what is preventing commitment

Success Criteria: By month 6, makes timely decisions under uncertainty and documents assumptions rather than waiting for certainty. Fewer decisions deferred to Lead Architect for resolution.

reflectiveQuestions: How much of your time do you currently spend developing other architects versus doing architecture yourself? Is the balance appropriate for your level?
Think about the best mentor or coach you have had. What made them effective? How can you replicate those qualities in your own mentoring?
Is there an architect in your team or community who has potential but is not developing? What is preventing their growth, and what could you do about it?
How would you handle a situation where someone you are mentoring makes a significant architecture mistake? How do you provide feedback without destroying their confidence?
If you left your current role tomorrow, could the architecture capability continue without you? If not, what do you need to do about that?

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the DDaT Capability Framework expect of architects at senior and lead levels?
options: Producing more architecture documents and diagrams than mid-level architects
Mentoring others, setting standards, and developing the capability of the architecture community
Being the sole decision-maker for all architecture in their department
Having certifications in every relevant technology framework
knowledgeCheck.explanation: At senior and lead levels, the DDaT framework expects architects to mentor others, set standards, and develop collective capability. The shift is from doing the work to enabling others to do it well — multiplying impact through the people you develop rather than through your individual output.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the difference between mentoring and coaching?
options: Mentoring is for junior staff and coaching is for senior staff
Mentoring focuses on long-term career development while coaching focuses on specific skills or challenges
Mentoring requires formal accreditation while coaching does not
There is no meaningful difference between them
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Mentoring is a longer-term relationship focused on career development, professional growth, and navigating organisational challenges. Coaching is more focused on developing specific skills or addressing specific challenges. Both are valuable and senior architects should use both approaches depending on what the developing architect needs.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most effective way to develop someone's architecture decision-making capability?
options: Telling them the correct answer whenever they face a decision
Sending them on a decision-making training course
Creating stretch assignments where they must make decisions with support available but not imposed
Having them read case studies of other architects' decisions
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Decision-making develops through practice with appropriate support. Stretch assignments create situations where the developing architect must exercise judgement, while knowing that support is available if needed. This builds real capability through experience rather than theoretical knowledge from courses or reading alone.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the most important outcome of a community of practice for architects?
options: Producing documentation that satisfies governance requirements
Collective learning that improves the quality of architecture across the team
Providing a social activity for the architecture team
Creating a forum for escalating problems to senior leadership
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Communities of practice exist to develop collective capability through shared learning. Activities like design crits, knowledge sharing, pair architecting, and decision retrospectives all serve this goal. The community improves architecture quality across the team — not just for individuals.

knowledgeCheck.question: When a less experienced architect brings you a problem, what is usually the most developmental response?
options: Solve it for them quickly so they can move on
Tell them to figure it out themselves without any guidance
Ask questions that help them explore options and develop their own judgement
Escalate it to a governance board for a formal decision
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Asking questions ('What options have you considered? What are the trade-offs? What would happen if...?') develops the person's decision-making capability. Solving it for them builds dependency. Leaving them entirely alone risks failure without learning. Coaching through questions builds the judgement they need to handle future problems independently.
